title: Crop Steering Academy
description: Learn the root zone, understand a watering day, and practise each control before live operation.

lessons.title: Before the buttons: water, roots and air
lessons.summary: Start with the pot: roots need access to water and oxygen. A sensor describes only a small part of the root zone.
outcomes: Identify solids, water and air in the substrate.
Explain why more water is not always better.
State one limit of a local sensor reading.

slides.title: The question
body: Before the buttons
Before you use the dashboard, identify the conditions inside the pot.
slides.narration:
Before you use the dashboard, identify the conditions inside the pot.

What do the roots need?

visual.title: The question
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Inside the root zone
body: Solids · water · air
The pot contains solid material, water, and air.
slides.narration:
Picture a handful of gravel. The pieces are solid, but there are gaps between them. A pot also contains solid material and spaces. The growing material around the roots is called substrate; coco and stone wool are examples.

Those spaces can contain water or air. Roots take up water, and they also need oxygen. Filling every space with water leaves less room for air.

So pouring in more water is not always helpful. The substrate needs to hold water, let excess drain away, and allow air back into some spaces.

visual.title: Inside the root zone
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.
visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

slides.title: Watch water arrive and drain
body: Some stays. Some drains.
Look at the spare container.
slides.narration:
Look at the spare container. Water enters the substrate. Some water stays in the substrate. Other water drains into the tray.

The amount of water then decreases. The plant uses some water. Evaporation and drainage also remove water.

A decrease in water content does not show only the water that the plant used.

visual.title: Watch water arrive and drain
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.
visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

slides.title: Pause before adding water
body: More water — or check first?
This pot stays very wet.
slides.narration:
This pot stays very wet. The leaves look unhealthy. Does this mean that you must add more water?

Choose one answer. Add more water immediately. Or do a check to find the cause first.

Do a check first.

Different problems can cause similar symptoms. The graph gives useful information. It does not identify every problem in the roots.

slides.title: What steering and sensing can do
body: Measure · check · observe
Crop steering means control of conditions to influence crop growth.
slides.narration:
Think of driving a car: you make adjustments to keep it on course. Crop steering means adjusting growing conditions to influence growth. Here we focus on irrigation, which means supplying water to the crop.

With irrigation, you choose when water arrives, how much arrives, and how long to wait before the next delivery. Light, temperature and humidity also change how much water the crop needs.

Later we will name two steering directions: vegetative and generative. They describe management intended to influence leafy growth or reproductive development. Neither guarantees yield. Drying the pot as much as possible is not the goal; roots must keep working.

A thermometer in one room cannot tell you the temperature in every room. A moisture sensor has the same local limit: one reading does not describe every pot or prove every dripper is clear.

Use sensor readings with equipment checks and crop observations.

Practise in the demo first; it does not operate a real pump. For a new installation, start with one zone: a group of plants whose water delivery is controlled together.

Point to the solid material in the drawing. Point to the water. Point to the air. Give one example of information that the sensor cannot supply.

The next lesson explains volumetric water content, or VWC.

lessons.title: VWC: what does 60% actually mean?
lessons.summary: Use equal volumes to understand volumetric water content, then separate VWC from plant-available water.
outcomes: Explain VWC as water volume divided by total measured sample volume.
Interpret 60% VWC without treating it as usable-water percentage.
Name the solids and air within the remaining volume.

slides.title: Recall before the reveal
body: Name the three parts
The previous lesson showed three parts inside the pot.
slides.narration:
The previous lesson showed three parts inside the pot.

Name these parts before the answer appears.

visual.title: Recall before the reveal
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Six out of ten
body: 60% VWC = 6 / 10 by volume
The three parts are solid material, water, and air.
slides.narration:
The three parts are solid material, water, and air.

Think of ten equal boxes making up the whole sample. How many boxes worth of water are inside it? That is the idea behind volumetric water content, or VWC: water volume divided by total sample volume, shown as a percentage.

In the drawing, water takes up six of the ten equal volumes. Six divided by ten is zero point six. Multiply by one hundred: sixty percent.

The blocks make the arithmetic visible. In real substrate, that water is spread through spaces between solid parts. It does not sit in six separate water blocks.

visual.title: Six out of ten
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.
visual.alt: Ten equal total volumes: six water, two solid material and two air. A 60% VWC example.

slides.title: Put litres beside the fraction
body: This example uses a representative sample with a total volume of five liters.
slides.narration:
Use a larger example: a total substrate sample of five litres at sixty percent VWC. Five times zero point six is three, so this sample contains three litres of water.

Imagine labelling the sample: three litres of water already inside. That label is not a watering instruction. It does not tell you to pour another three litres into a five litre pot.

visual.title: Put litres beside the fraction
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: The probe sees a region
body: Local reading ≠ entire zone
Sixty percent of the total volume is water.
slides.narration:
Sixty percent of the total volume is water. Is all the remaining forty percent air?

No. The remaining volume includes solid material and air. VWC alone does not give the complete air volume.

Do not read VWC like a fuel gauge showing how much usable fuel remains. Water in substrate is not all equally easy for roots to take up. Some is held more tightly. The same VWC in different substrates can mean different conditions for the plant.

Look at the probe. Its position and contact with the substrate matter. Calibration means checking how its output relates to the quantity being measured. These things affect whether the local reading is trustworthy.

A probe near one dripper might not represent a dry pot at the end of a row. Later lessons explain how to select locations that represent the zone.

visual.title: The probe sees a region
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Teach it back
body: What does 60% mean?
The sensor now shows forty percent VWC.
slides.narration:
The sensor now shows forty percent VWC. Does this reading always mean that the substrate is too dry?

No. Forty percent in one substrate can mean something different in another. Use your substrate, checked reference values, crop and current conditions to interpret it. There is no single VWC target for every system.

Do not select a target yet. Complete this sentence. Sixty percent VWC means what?

Approximately sixty percent of the measured sample volume is water. This is one correct answer.

The reading does not give the exact water volume available to the plant. One sensor does not prove that all pots have the same conditions.

Use these limits when you assess advice about VWC.

Next, a kitchen sponge will help explain saturation, water left after drainage, and the reference number in the app.

options.feedback: That interpretation confuses measured water content with plant-available water.

options.text: No. It describes water volume in the measured sample.
options.feedback: Plant availability depends on more than that volume fraction.

options.text: Yes. Water and air are the only components.
options.feedback: Recall the solid growing material introduced in A1.

options.text: No. The remainder also includes solid material.
options.feedback: Total substrate volume includes solids, water and air.

options.text: Treat the change as litres consumed by all plants.
options.feedback: A local volume fraction is not a zone water meter or uptake measurement.

options.text: Check the identified probe, units, time and context.
options.feedback: The line describes sampled water content; evidence still matters.

lessons.title: The sponge, the pot and the Post-it
lessons.summary: Use a kitchen sponge to understand saturation, water left after drainage, and why an app reference cannot change the water in a pot.
outcomes: Explain the difference between a dripping sponge and a wet sponge after drainage.
Calculate 60% VWC from 600 mL of water in a 1 L total substrate sample.
Explain why editing the app reference does not add or remove water.

slides.title: Start with a kitchen sponge
body: Dunk, lift, drip
Water fills spaces. The sponge material stays.
slides.narration:
Dunk a kitchen sponge, then lift it out, dripping. Water fills the spaces inside it. Picture that as saturation.

The sponge material has not vanished. In substrate, water also fills spaces between solids. Saturation does not mean one hundred percent of the total sample is water.

visual.title: Start with a kitchen sponge
labels: Water fills spaces. The sponge material stays.
visual.caption: Conceptual sponge analogy. The 60% VWC calculation is an illustration, not a target.
visual.alt: A soaked sponge and a still-wet sponge after excess water drains.

slides.title: Let it drip, without squeezing
body: Still wet after drainage
Excess water leaves. Air returns to some spaces.
slides.narration:
Hold the sponge over the sink. Do not squeeze it. Let the excess water drip away. It still feels wet, but some spaces now contain air again.

Soaked and dripping, then wet after drainage: those are two different conditions. The same distinction matters in a pot, where roots need both water and oxygen.

visual.title: Let it drip, without squeezing
labels: Excess water leaves. Air returns to some spaces.
visual.caption: Conceptual sponge analogy. The 60% VWC calculation is an illustration, not a target.
visual.alt: Let excess water drain without squeezing. Water remains and air returns to some spaces.

slides.title: From the sponge to the pot
body: Check your own container
Repeat the conditions. Example: 600 mL water in 1 L total sample = 60% VWC.
slides.narration:
Now wet a spare container of substrate. Let excess water drain using a suitable, repeatable check. Do not squeeze the substrate.

The water left after that check is its container capacity: water held under those particular container and drainage conditions.

Tall and shallow containers can retain different amounts. Substrate matters too. One sponge cannot tell you what every pot holds.

This drainage check describes container capacity. The app also has a field capacity reference. Check how it is set: automatic updates can follow observed wet peaks. A wet peak alone is not a drained-container measurement.

Repeat with the same substrate, container, starting condition and drainage procedure. There is no single drainage time for every setup.

Check probe placement and contact. Compare its reading with container weight and drainage. A number alone cannot show that the check worked.

Example: a one litre total substrate sample contains six hundred millilitres of water. Six hundred divided by one thousand is sixty percent VWC: volumetric water content.

visual.title: From the sponge to the pot
labels: Repeat the conditions. Example: 600 mL water in 1 L total sample = 60% VWC.
visual.caption: Conceptual sponge analogy. The 60% VWC calculation is an illustration, not a target.
visual.alt: Conceptual container cutaway: excess water drains; water and air remain among solids.

slides.title: A Post-it cannot add water
body: The app reference is a note
Changing the number does not add water.
slides.narration:
Imagine writing that sixty percent on a Post-it beside the sponge. Changing the Post-it to seventy percent would not add a drop of water.

The app reference works like that note. It tells the program which number to use. The edit itself adds no water.

visual.title: A Post-it cannot add water
labels: The app reference is a note
Changing the number does not add water.
visual.caption: Conceptual sponge analogy. The 60% VWC calculation is an illustration, not a target.
visual.alt: An unchanged wet sponge beside a reference note. A software reference cannot add water.

slides.title: Change the note: what happens?
body: Think before the answer
What changes physically when you edit the reference?
slides.narration:
You change the app reference from sixty to seventy percent. What happens to the water already in the pot?

Nothing. You changed the note, not the water. A physical change needs water to enter or leave.

And sixty percent was only our worked example. Your own container check could give a different result.

The highest spike on a graph is not automatically the drained reference. It could be a brief wet peak or a bad reading.

Think back to the sponge: dripping wet, then wet after excess water drains, then a note describing it.

The first two describe physical conditions. The note, like the app setting, describes a reference supported by a suitable check.

Next comes dryback: water content falls as water leaves. Keep the sponge and its Post-it separate mentally.

visual.title: Change the note: what happens?
labels: What changes physically when you edit the reference?
visual.caption: Conceptual sponge analogy. The 60% VWC calculation is an illustration, not a target.

practice.prompt: Use a kitchen sponge over a sink: soak it, lift it dripping, then let excess water drain without squeezing. Describe what changed. Write a number on a note beside it, then change the number. Did the sponge gain water? Explain how this maps to a pot and the app reference.
hints: After dripping, the sponge still holds water and some spaces contain air.
A note describes a condition; it cannot change that condition.
practice.success: You distinguish saturation from water retained after drainage, and explain that changing the reference number cannot add or remove water. A pot needs its own suitable, repeatable container check.

quiz.prompt: A soaked sponge is dripping. How does that help explain saturation?

options.text: Water fills the spaces; solid material remains.
options.feedback: Correct. Water fills pore spaces, while solid material still occupies part of the total volume.

options.text: The entire sample has become water, so VWC must be 100%.
options.feedback: The sponge material, like substrate solids, has not vanished. Saturation does not mean the total sample is all water.

quiz.prompt: You let the sponge drip without squeezing. What does the wet sponge help you picture?

options.text: All its water has gone.
options.feedback: It is still wet. Excess water left and air returned to some spaces.

options.text: Water remains while some spaces contain air again.
options.feedback: That is the idea to carry into a container capacity check. The pot needs its own suitable drainage procedure.

quiz.prompt: A 1 L total substrate sample contains 600 mL water. What is its VWC?

options.text: 60%; this example does not set every pot's target.
options.feedback: 600 divided by 1000, multiplied by 100, is 60%. Your own substrate and container need a suitable check.

options.text: 100%, because the sample was watered.
options.feedback: VWC compares water volume with total sample volume: 600 / 1000 = 60%.

quiz.prompt: You edit the app reference from 60% to 70%. What happens to water already in the pot?

options.text: It immediately rises to 70%.
options.feedback: Changing the Post-it cannot wet the sponge. Changing a setting cannot add water to the pot.

options.text: Nothing physically; only the reference number changes.
options.feedback: Water must enter or leave for the physical water content to change. A useful reference is supported by a suitable container check.

instructions: Use a kitchen sponge over a sink: soak it, lift it dripping, then let excess water drain without squeezing. Describe what changed. Write a number on a note beside it, then change the number. Did the sponge gain water? Explain how this maps to a pot and the app reference.
Teach back the difference between the physical water and the reference number.

lessons.title: Dryback without the confusing maths
lessons.summary: Use a familiar balance to understand a fall in water content, then calculate and label dryback.
outcomes: Explain dryback as a fall between two water-content readings.
Calculate percentage points and relative dryback from the starting reading.
Read the meaning of a program field before using its number.

slides.title: Think of a bank balance
body: A balance falls from 60 to 45: the decrease is 15.
Dryback describes a fall in measured water content.
slides.narration: Imagine a bank balance falling from sixty dollars to forty-five. Fifteen dollars has gone. Now replace dollars with readings from the same water-content probe. Water content has fallen between two times. Growers call that fall dryback. The calculation describes the change. It cannot tell us how much went into the plant, drained away, or evaporated.

visual.title: Think of a bank balance
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: First find the size of the fall
body: Start 60% VWC; end 45% VWC.
60 − 45 = 15 percentage points.
slides.narration: VWC means the share of the measured sample volume occupied by water. Our example starts at sixty percent VWC and ends at forty-five percent. Subtract forty-five from sixty. The fall is fifteen percentage points. The word points matters because we are subtracting two percentage readings. Keep the starting reading and its time beside the ending reading.

visual.title: First find the size of the fall
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Describe a fall from 60% to 45% VWC.
steps: Subtract: 60 - 45 = 15 percentage points.
Divide the drop by the starting value: 15 / 60 = 0.25.
Multiply by 100: relative dryback = 25%.

slides.title: Then compare the fall with the start
body: Drop / starting reading × 100
15 / 60 × 100 = 25% relative dryback.
slides.narration: How large was that fall compared with the starting amount? Divide fifteen by sixty. That is one quarter. Multiply by one hundred to get twenty-five percent relative dryback. So this same fall is fifteen percentage points, or twenty-five percent of its start. Always divide by the starting reading for this calculation. A zero start cannot be used.

visual.title: Then compare the fall with the start
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
body: Start 80%; end 60%.
80 − 60 = __ points.
__ / 80 × 100 = __% relative dryback.
slides.narration: Try the next example with help. Start at eighty percent VWC and finish at sixty. First subtract the end from the start. Then divide that answer by eighty and multiply by one hundred. Pause and write both answers. The fall is twenty percentage points. The relative dryback is twenty-five percent. Label each answer so another person can follow it.

visual.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try it without the steps
body: Start 50%; end 40%.
Write both labelled answers before continuing.
slides.narration: Now use fifty percent to forty percent VWC. Work it out before continuing. The fall is ten percentage points. Ten divided by fifty, multiplied by one hundred, is twenty percent relative dryback. A useful record includes both readings, their times, and the labelled calculation. VWC describes water volume in the sampled region, rather than the percentage of usable water left.

visual.title: Try it without the steps
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Read the field before entering a number
body: Peak 60%; requested relative loss 10%.
10% of 60 = 6 points; reference = 54% VWC.
slides.narration: The program uses relative dryback for its morning reference. With a sixty percent peak, a ten percent relative loss is six points. Sixty minus six gives a fifty-four percent VWC reference. Read the field help before entering a value. The reference tells the program what to compare against. The probe reading tells you what was observed.

visual.title: Read the field before entering a number
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Recall the method
body: Find the start, end and interval.
Subtract; then divide by the start for the relative result.
slides.narration: Cover the examples and explain the method aloud. What are the starting and ending readings? What interval separates them? First subtract. For relative dryback, divide that fall by the start and multiply by one hundred. Finish the practice with new numbers. Before using a real record, check that its probe, units and timestamps match the situation you are describing.

visual.title: Recall the method
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: Calculate both dryback descriptions for 70% to 56% VWC. Then find the VWC reference for 10% relative dryback from a 50% peak.
hints: Subtract the end from the start.
For relative dryback, divide the drop by the start and multiply by 100.
practice.success: 14 percentage points; 20% relative dryback; 45% VWC reference. Name the starting value used in each relative calculation.

quiz.prompt: A reading falls from 50% to 40% VWC. Which description is correct?

options.text: 10 percentage points and 20% relative dryback
options.feedback: The drop is 10 points; 10 / 50 × 100 is 20%.

options.text: 10 percentage points and 10% relative dryback
options.feedback: Ten is the point difference. The relative result uses 50 as the denominator and is 20%.

options.text: 20 percentage points and 10% relative dryback
options.feedback: Subtract first: 50 - 40 is 10 points. Dividing 10 by 50 gives 20%.

quiz.prompt: A 60% peak loses 10% of its starting value. What is the resulting VWC?

options.feedback: That subtracts 10 percentage points. A relative loss is 10% of 60, which is 6 points.
The loss is 6 points, so 60 - 6 = 54% VWC.
Six is the point loss. Subtract it from the starting reading to obtain the ending VWC.

quiz.prompt: Why is the note “15% dryback” incomplete?

options.text: It needs a higher target.
options.feedback: The problem is missing meaning, not target size. State points or relative percentage and the interval.

options.text: It does not state the calculation convention.
options.feedback: Fifteen points and 15% of a starting value usually give different ending readings.

options.text: Dryback can only be expressed in points.
options.feedback: Both points and relative percentage are useful when clearly labelled.

quiz.prompt: What does a 60% VWC reading establish?

options.text: Exactly 60% of usable water remains.
options.feedback: VWC is water volume divided by total measured sample volume. Availability is a different property.

options.text: Every pot has the same water content.
options.feedback: A probe samples a local region. Other pots may differ.

options.text: About 60% of the measured sample volume is water.
options.feedback: That is the VWC definition from A2; it does not establish availability or zone uniformity.

Repeat with 50% to 40%, then check your answers.
Use no live irrigation settings for this exercise.

lessons.title: EC: what it measures, and which EC you are looking at
lessons.summary: Understand EC using salted water, then identify where each conductivity measurement comes from.
outcomes: Explain EC as electrical conductivity without treating it as a nutrient analysis.
Distinguish supplied solution, bulk substrate, pore water and collected drainage.
Label a reading with its type, unit and method before comparing it.

slides.title: Start with salted water
body: Dissolved salts affect how easily water carries electrical current.
EC is short for electrical conductivity.
slides.narration: Think of making salted water stronger by dissolving more salt in it. A conductivity meter responds to how easily electrical current passes through that water. EC is short for electrical conductivity. It is a useful clue about dissolved salts. It does not list the amount of each nutrient. Keep the material being measured and its unit beside the number.

visual.title: Start with salted water
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.
visual.alt: Conceptual conductivity comparison: dissolved salts carry electrical charge in water.

slides.title: Ask where the reading came from
body: Feed: solution being supplied.
Bulk: the wet substrate around a probe.
Pore water: water between substrate particles.
Runoff or extract: a collected sample.
slides.narration: Follow the water. In the supply tank, we call the solution reading feed EC. A probe in the wet substrate can measure bulk EC: the combined material around it. Pore-water EC describes the water between the particles. Runoff is collected drainage. A laboratory extract uses its own collection procedure. These names describe different measurements, even when the units match.

visual.title: Ask where the reading came from
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: label two readings
body: Tank: feed EC 2.0 mS/cm.
TEROS 12 direct output: bulk EC 0.8 mS/cm.
slides.narration: Our tank sample reads two point zero millisiemens per centimetre. That unit is written mS slash cm. Label the record feed EC. The direct conductivity output from a TEROS twelve probe reads zero point eight in the same unit. Label it bulk EC. The difference alone does not diagnose a problem. The tank solution and the wet substrate are different things.

visual.title: Worked example: label two readings
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Label a tank reading of 2.0 mS/cm and a TEROS 12 direct conductivity reading of 0.8 mS/cm.
steps: Find where each sample or measurement came from.
Label the supplied solution feed EC.
Label the direct TEROS 12 conductivity output bulk EC.
workedExample.answer: Feed EC 2.0 mS/cm; bulk EC 0.8 mS/cm. The difference alone does not diagnose nutrition.

slides.title: A calculated value needs a method
body: Bulk EC → documented calculation → estimated pore-water EC.
Renaming a value does not convert it.
slides.narration: Some software estimates pore-water EC from bulk measurements. An estimate uses a calculation with required inputs and a range where it is reliable. Find that documented method before interpreting the result. Changing the display name does not perform the calculation. If the measurement type is unknown, record it as unknown while you trace its source.

visual.title: A calculated value needs a method
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Your turn: finish the labels
body: Supplied solution: feed EC.
Collected drainage: __ EC.
Water between particles: __ EC.
slides.narration: Finish these labels aloud. The supplied solution is feed EC. A cup collected under a stated drainage procedure is what? Water in the spaces between particles is what? Pause first. The answers are runoff EC and pore-water EC. Keep the drainage collection method with the result. Use the same measurement type and method when following a trend.

visual.title: Your turn: finish the labels
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try a fresh record
body: Supply 1.7 mS/cm; drainage cup 2.4 mS/cm.
Label both before interpreting their difference.
slides.narration: Try a supply reading of one point seven and a drainage reading of two point four, both in millisiemens per centimetre. Write feed EC and runoff EC beside them. Before interpreting the difference, check collection timing, the meter check, and temperature adjustment. These two numbers cannot identify a particular excessive nutrient or describe every part of every pot.

visual.title: Try a fresh record
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Recall what the labels mean
body: What material? Which unit? Which method?
VWC describes water volume; EC describes conductivity.
slides.narration: Cover the labels and name the four measurement locations again. EC describes conductivity. VWC describes the share of sample volume occupied by water. Neither is a direct measurement of how much water a plant can access. Keep each reading in its crop and substrate context. A useful comparison starts with the same kind of measurement, rather than a universal number to copy.

visual.title: Recall what the labels mean
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

practice.prompt: Label these new samples: supply solution at 1.9 mS/cm; direct TEROS 12 output at 0.6 mS/cm; water extracted by a stated laboratory procedure at 2.7 mS/cm. Explain why these numbers cannot identify an individual deficient nutrient.
hints: Start with sample location, not number size.

options.text: Bulk EC

lessons.title: Can you trust that reading?
lessons.summary: Check a reading as you would check a thermometer and a dated photograph: where it came from, when it arrived and whether it is reliable.
outcomes: Separate freshness, correct identity and measurement accuracy.
Calculate reading age and recognise the VWC fraction-to-percent conversion.
Choose a supported check when a reading is unreliable.

slides.title: A reading is a dated local observation
body: Thermometer: which room?
Photograph: taken when?
Probe: is the measurement reliable?
slides.narration: A thermometer in the hallway cannot tell you the exact temperature in a bedroom. Yesterday’s photograph cannot show what the room looks like now. Treat a probe reading in the same way. Ask three separate questions. Is this the right location? Is the observation recent? Is the measurement reliable? A believable number can still fail one of those checks.

visual.title: A reading is a dated local observation
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.
visual.alt: A probe observes a small local region. Other pots and distant parts of the medium may differ.

slides.title: Worked example: how old is it?
body: Now 14:00; probe A last observed at 10:00.
A is four hours old; probe B at 13:59 is one minute old.
slides.narration: The clock says two in the afternoon, or fourteen hundred. Probe A last supplied a valid observation at ten in the morning. Its reading is four hours old. Probe B updated at thirteen fifty-nine, one minute ago. We have calculated their ages. We have not established the current water content at A. A flat line might be steady conditions or missing updates.

visual.title: Worked example: how old is it?
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: At 14:00, probe A last updated at 10:00. What is the first finding?
steps: Confirm the timestamp belongs to the last valid observation.
Subtract 10:00 from 14:00.
Record four-hour-old data and investigate its source.
workedExample.answer: Probe A has four-hour-old data. The record cannot establish current water content.

slides.title: Check identity and units
body: Match the physical probe label to the displayed record.
0.45 m³/m³ = 45% VWC.
slides.narration: Next find the probe’s physical label and match it to the displayed room and zone. Then check units. A source value of zero point four five cubic metres per cubic metre is a fraction. Multiply by one hundred to display forty-five percent VWC. Reading it as zero point four five percent would create a hundredfold scale error.

visual.title: Check identity and units
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: A fresh reading can still be inaccurate
body: Placement: where the probe samples.
Calibration: how its signal becomes a reported value.
slides.narration: Accuracy is a separate question from age. Calibration is the method used to turn the sensor signal into a reported measurement. It must suit the sensor and substrate. Placement matters too. Air gaps near moisture-sensor needles can produce misleading readings. A probe near one dripper also samples a different place from the far side of the pot. Check the installation record.

visual.title: A fresh reading can still be inaccurate
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.
visual.alt: Check local probe position and contact; a fresh value cannot establish whole-zone accuracy.

slides.title: Your turn: calculate, then check
body: Now 15:30; last valid observation 15:25.
Age = __ minutes. What does age alone establish?
slides.narration: It is fifteen thirty. The last valid observation was at fifteen twenty-five. Pause and calculate its age. The answer is five minutes. That answers freshness only. It does not prove the probe is correctly identified or calibrated. With the identity and units checked, look for suitable placement and calibration records. A recent reading still needs a trustworthy measurement behind it.

visual.title: Your turn: calculate, then check
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try a changed scenario
body: At 16:20: A shows 48% from 12:20.
B shows 43% from 16:19.
slides.narration: Now compare forty-eight percent from twelve twenty with forty-three percent from sixteen nineteen. The current time is sixteen twenty. A is four hours old; B is one minute old. Check identities and last valid timestamps first. Then investigate availability and communications. Follow with appropriate physical evidence. The difference alone does not establish that every pot needs water.

visual.title: Try a changed scenario
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Recall the three questions
body: Right probe? Recent observation? Reliable measurement?
Record a fault and use the local fallback procedure.
slides.narration: Explain the three questions without looking: right probe, recent observation, reliable measurement. If sensing fails, record what you know and involve the responsible operator using the local fallback procedure. Lowering a protection to force irrigation leaves the sensing fault unresolved. Finish with a check record that separates the observation, its age, and the next step needed to trust it.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

quiz.prompt: Two probes agree. What does their agreement prove?

options.text: The whole zone is uniform.
options.feedback: Two local samples do not prove every container or location is the same.

options.text: Calibration must be correct.
options.feedback: Both probes may share a calibration or placement error.

options.text: Their reported values agree; other checks are still needed.
options.feedback: Agreement is useful evidence, alongside identity, freshness, calibration and placement.

options.text: Lower a protection to force a shot.
options.feedback: That bypasses the fault instead of restoring trustworthy evidence. Follow the safe fallback procedure.

options.text: Investigate sensing and follow the local safe fallback procedure.
options.feedback: Resolve identity, freshness, communication and physical evidence with the responsible operator.

options.text: Treat the old number as a current measurement.
options.feedback: An old value does not establish the current condition.

options.feedback: A volume fraction of 0.45 becomes 45% when multiplied by 100.
The fraction and percentage express the same water-to-sample volume ratio.
That is a scale error. Multiply 0.45 by 100 to obtain 45%.

lessons.title: Read water and EC on the same graph
lessons.summary: Read both axes, find day and night, and keep recorded evidence separate from a planning reference.
outcomes: Locate time, VWC and EC axes on a combined chart.
Identify shots, the night period and missing or stale evidence.
Explain why a draft reference can move while recorded data remain unchanged.

slides.title: Start with time
body: Time moves to the right
This graph shows water content and EC over time.
slides.narration:
Think of a car dashboard: the speedometer and fuel gauge share one panel, but tell you different things. This graph puts water content and EC on one screen. We will learn what each line means.

Read time along the bottom, like a diary laid out from left to right. Farther right means later. The shaded section is night in this example. The sensors can keep measuring through it.

visual.title: Start with time
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Add water content
body: VWC uses the left axis (%)
The first line shows VWC.
slides.narration:
Start with the blue line: VWC, or water content by volume. Read its height against the percentage scale on the left. Use the time below to find when that reading happened.

At this example point, the reading is sixty percent VWC. The solid line joins the observations so you can follow the change over time.

A stale weather report cannot tell you the weather now. Check the age of live readings and look for missing sections. A smooth-looking line does not prove fresh, complete measurements.

visual.title: Add water content
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Add EC and a second scale
body: EC uses the right axis (mS/cm)
EC means electrical conductivity.
slides.narration:
Imagine a tiny electrical test through a sample. Dissolved salts help carry the current. EC, electrical conductivity, measures how readily current passes. Read EC on the right-hand scale, in millisiemens per centimetre.

Before interpreting EC, ask where it was measured. A number from the tank does not automatically describe the water around the roots.

Feed EC describes the irrigation solution. Bulk substrate EC measures the combined substrate region. Pore-water EC describes water in the spaces between solids. These are different measurements; identify which one your graph actually shows.

Now the two lines cross on screen. Think of the speedometer needle and fuel-gauge needle pointing the same way. Would that make speed equal fuel? Do crossing VWC and EC lines mean equal measurements?

No. One uses percent on the left; the other uses conductivity units on the right. Their screen positions depend on those scales. Follow how each measurement changes over time.

Subtracting EC from VWC would be like subtracting litres from kilometres per hour. The quantities and units do not match. EC alone is not a complete nutrient recipe either.

visual.title: Add EC and a second scale
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Events, observations and references
body: Observed ≠ reference
The markers show irrigation events.
slides.narration:
On this teaching chart, delivery markers show when watering started. In the app, a dot marks a shot start; a ring marks a shot the watering software held. Neither alone measures water delivered. VWC may rise after water reaches the probe, then fall between deliveries.

EC does not have to mirror VWC. Delivery, mixing, drainage, temperature, measurement method and crop conditions can affect it. Seeing two changes together does not prove that one caused the other.

Think of a journey plan beside the trip you actually drove. The dashed planning reference comes from software settings. The measured line shows observations. They need different labels even if they happen to follow the same path.

visual.title: Events, observations and references
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Continue into night; move a threshold
body: Draft floor moves; observations stay
The planning reference continues through the night to the next morning.
slides.narration:
Follow the planning line through the shaded night to the next morning. Like a route drawn on a map, it should be readable across the whole journey. A continuous line is still only a reference, not proof of tomorrow's crop response.

Here the EC reference joins the last daytime reference to the next morning reference. The overnight phase is called P3. This join is not a separately scheduled P3 EC target, and it does not calculate how salts will behave overnight.

Now watch this demo edit. We increase the P3 emergency VWC threshold in the local draft. The draft threshold changes from thirty-five percent to thirty-nine percent. The saved threshold remains visible for comparison. The measured example readings remain the same.

visual.title: Continue into night; move a threshold
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Explain what changed
body: A draft, not a guaranteed shot
Which item changed?
slides.narration:
Which item changed? The previous water content? The local draft of a threshold? Or a guaranteed irrigation event?

Only the local draft changed. Think of a fridge alarm limit: it marks an exceptional condition, not the normal temperature you aim for. This emergency water threshold is not a normal overnight target. Review and apply are separate actions; the watering software, called the Controller, still checks its conditions and protection rules before irrigation.

Point to the time axis. Point to the VWC scale. Point to the EC scale. Identify one irrigation marker. Identify one planning reference. Find the reading age.

The next lesson explains the irrigation phases from P0 to P3.

visual.title: Explain what changed
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

options.feedback: Line crossings do not make their units equivalent.

options.text: The left axis, in percent.
options.feedback: The EC line has its own right-hand conductivity axis.

options.text: The recorded VWC curve moves to match.
options.feedback: Changing a target cannot rewrite sensor measurements.

options.text: It stays unchanged.
options.feedback: A draft is a proposed setting; recorded evidence is separate.

quiz.prompt: A smooth flat trace has an old timestamp. What next?

options.text: Assume the crop is perfectly stable.
options.feedback: Appearance is not proof that readings are current.

options.text: Investigate freshness and identity before acting on it.
options.feedback: A convincing line can still be stale.

options.text: That the program actively holds a scheduled P3 EC target.
options.feedback: The illustrative line is not proof of an independent EC control loop.

options.text: Only a reference connection between illustrated endpoints.
options.feedback: There is no independent scheduled P3 EC target or guaranteed EC forecast.

lessons.title: P0 to P3: build the day one phase at a time
lessons.summary: Follow a watering day as four familiar jobs: wait, refill, maintain and allow dryback; then attach the program’s P0–P3 labels.
outcomes: Put wait, refill, maintain and overnight dryback in order.
Match those purposes to this program’s P0, P1, P2 and P3 phases.
Explain why projected events and an emergency reference do not guarantee watering.

slides.title: Four jobs across the watering day
body: Wait in the morning → refill → maintain → allow overnight dryback.
The program labels these P0 → P1 → P2 → P3.
slides.narration: Think of the watering day as a journey with four jobs. Wait while the root zone dries in the morning. Refill with watering events. Maintain water content during the active period. Then allow dryback overnight. The program labels these jobs: P zero, P one, P two and P three. A phase simply means one part of that sequence.

visual.title: Four jobs across the watering day
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Wait first: morning dryback, P0
body: At configured lights-on, the new grow-day starts in P0.
Dryback and timing rules decide when the refill can begin.
slides.narration: The first job is waiting. At configured lights-on, a new grow-day begins in P zero, called morning dryback. Water content can continue falling before refill begins. The controller checks the dryback rule and timing limits, including a maximum wait. Lights-on alone therefore does not supply an exact first-shot time. Match the configured lighting schedule with the room.

visual.title: Wait first: morning dryback, P0
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Refill: ramp-up, P1
body: A shot is one watering event.
P1 uses shots and checks to approach a configured target.
slides.narration: The second job is refill. The program calls it P one, or ramp-up. A shot means one watering event. Several shots can raise water content toward the configured target, with checks between events. The target is a comparison value used by the rule. The probe response also depends on delivery and drainage. Count completed events from records rather than from a drawing.

visual.title: Refill: ramp-up, P1
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Maintain: conditional watering, P2
body: P2 checks a re-water threshold.
A threshold is a value used to decide whether another shot is needed.
slides.narration: The third job is maintenance, called P two. A re-water threshold is the reference used when deciding whether another shot is needed. Readings, timing rules and protections still apply. A planning chart may show evenly spaced shots using an assumed drying rate. If actual drying is slower, fewer events may occur. Read the controller’s reason before calling a missing shot a fault.

visual.title: Maintain: conditional watering, P2
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: a 06:00–18:00 lighting day
body: 06:00: configured lights-on and start of the grow-day.
Wait → refill → maintain → overnight dryback.
Lighting hours do not fix every transition or shot time.
slides.narration: Use a fictional room lit from six in the morning to six in the evening. At six, begin the morning wait. When its rules allow, move to refill, then maintenance. Daytime watering can finish before lights-off. The overnight period follows. Explain those four jobs in order. We cannot calculate the refill and maintenance transition times from lighting hours alone.

visual.title: Worked example: a 06:00–18:00 lighting day
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Explain a 06:00–18:00 lighting day without inventing shot times.
steps: Place P0 at the start of the grow-day.
Describe P1 ramp-up and P2 maintenance by purpose.
Describe P3 overnight and its separate emergency floor.
workedExample.answer: The sequence explains rules and purposes. Lighting hours alone do not determine exact transitions or shot counts.

slides.title: Overnight dryback: P3
body: P3 covers the overnight period.
Its emergency floor is a separate rescue reference.
slides.narration: The fourth job is overnight dryback, called P three. The emergency floor is a separate low-water reference for the overnight rescue rule. It is not a nightly destination to aim for. A rescue event depends on its conditions and protections; the label overnight does not order an automatic night shot. Unreliable sensing needs the local fallback procedure and the responsible operator.

visual.title: Overnight dryback: P3
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Your turn: explain another day
body: Complete: wait = __; refill = P1; maintain = __; overnight = P3.
Then explain an 08:00–20:00 example.
slides.narration: Pause and fill the gaps. Morning wait is P zero. Maintenance is P two. Now explain a room lit from eight in the morning to eight in the evening using all four jobs. Which shot times remain unknown? Recall that a forecast describes assumed events, while the event record describes completed actions. Moving a reference line cannot change yesterday’s observed readings.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

options.text: P0 morning dryback → P1 ramp-up → P2 maintenance → P3 overnight

options.feedback: The projection uses a drying rate. Actual events depend on rules, fresh readings and protections.

options.text: Illustrative times under the projection’s assumptions.
options.feedback: Use actual event records to determine what happened.

options.text: Proof those shots already completed.
options.feedback: Actual event and delivery evidence are needed to support a claim about completed watering.

options.text: A routine nightly destination to chase.
options.feedback: It is a separate protection reference, not a routine moisture target.

options.text: Proof that a rescue shot must always occur.
options.feedback: The rescue rule still has conditions and protections. A threshold does not guarantee a shot.

options.text: A reference used by the overnight rescue rule.
options.feedback: Keep its protection role separate from ordinary targets and projected dryback.

options.text: Every P1 shot time.
options.feedback: Ramp timing also depends on configured rules and observed conditions.

options.text: The lighting period used as context for the grow-day.
options.feedback: Verify it matches the actual installation; it does not fully determine irrigation transitions.

options.text: The exact amount each plant takes up.
options.feedback: Lighting hours do not measure delivery or uptake.

lessons.title: Vegetative and generative: a bias, not a magic switch
lessons.summary: Use a dimmer-switch analogy to separate a steering direction from the planner’s numerical blend and the crop’s actual response.
outcomes: Explain vegetative and generative as intended directions, separate from growth stage.
Calculate a blend between two configured endpoint values.
Name the crop and substrate context needed to judge whether those settings suit a zone.

slides.title: Think of a dimmer
body: Vegetative: roots, leaves and shoots.
Generative: reproductive growth, such as flowers and fruit.
Bias means an intended direction.
slides.narration: A dimmer moves gradually between two ends of a range. Keep that picture for the planner slider. First name the directions. Vegetative growth includes roots, leaves and shoots. Generative growth includes reproductive structures, such as flowers and fruit. A steering bias is an intended influence on that balance. It is separate from the plant’s stage and does not guarantee a response.

visual.title: Think of a dimmer
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: The plant responds to its conditions
body: Irrigation timing, dryback and EC interact with climate and light.
The substrate, variety and crop stage affect the response.
slides.narration: Growers influence root-zone conditions through irrigation timing, dryback and suitable EC bounds. Climate and light also matter. In suitable conditions, smaller drybacks can support a vegetative direction; greater dryback can contribute to a generative direction. These are broad tendencies. Substrate, plant variety and stage change the response. A flowering plant may still need a vegetative bias to support balanced growth.

visual.title: The plant responds to its conditions
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: What the slider actually calculates
body: A profile stores two sets of operator-defined values.
0 selects the vegetative endpoint; 100 selects the generative endpoint.
slides.narration: An endpoint is a set of values at one end of the slider. A profile stores both sets for reuse. Zero selects the configured vegetative endpoint. One hundred selects the generative endpoint. Between them, the planner blends supported settings. The grower supplies the bounds. Pot size and dripper flow help describe the setup, but cannot choose the biological targets automatically.

visual.title: What the slider actually calculates
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Worked example: halfway
body: Fictional wait endpoints: 30 and 50 minutes.
slides.narration: Take fictional morning-wait endpoints of thirty and fifty minutes. Their difference is twenty. At slider fifty, use half the difference: ten minutes. Add ten to thirty. The result is forty minutes, before rounding to the setting’s supported step. This calculation explains the slider. Choosing suitable endpoints needs knowledge of the actual crop and substrate.

visual.title: Worked example: halfway
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Blend fictional endpoints of 30 and 50 minutes at slider 50.
steps: Difference: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes.
Fraction: 50 / 100 = 0.5.
Blend: 30 + 0.5 × 20 = 40 minutes, before parameter-step rounding.
workedExample.answer: 40 minutes in this arithmetic example. Endpoint suitability remains a separate local decision.

slides.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
body: Endpoints 30 and 50; slider 25.
Equal endpoints produce no change.
slides.narration: Keep thirty and fifty as the endpoints. Set the slider to twenty-five. What fraction of the difference is that? Pause and calculate. One quarter of twenty is five. Add five to thirty to get thirty-five minutes. If both endpoints were thirty, their difference would be zero. Moving the slider would then leave that setting at thirty.

visual.title: Your turn, with the steps supplied
labels: Calculate the blended time before continuing.
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Try a new pair independently
body: Endpoints 20 and 60 minutes; slider 75.
Calculate the blend before continuing.
slides.narration: Now try endpoints of twenty and sixty minutes at slider seventy-five. Work it out first. Their difference is forty. Three quarters of forty is thirty. Add thirty to twenty for fifty minutes. The slider number is a position along the range, rather than a time in minutes. This result predicts the configured blend, not the plant’s response.

visual.title: Try a new pair independently
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

slides.title: Recall the calculation and its scope
body: Check every supported setting and every schedule using a shared profile.
Previewing a change does not apply a plan.
slides.narration: Explain the dimmer analogy aloud, then name its limit: plants are not lamps with a guaranteed response. Check the whole profile, including the measurement type of any EC fields. A shared profile can serve several schedule blocks. A preview shows a draft; applying the plan is a separate workflow. Finish the practice by calculating first, then stating what the arithmetic cannot establish.

visual.title: Recall the calculation and its scope
visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

A zero endpoint difference gives zero change.

slides.title: A dripper is a small tap
body: Flow rate says how much water passes in a given time.
Each example emitter delivers 4 L/h; two serve each plant.
Rated flow is also called nominal flow.
slides.narration: Picture each dripper as a small tap. Its flow rate says how much water it delivers in a given time. Four litres per hour, written four L slash h, means four litres in one hour at that stated flow. Two such emitters supply each example plant. A rated flow is a label; a timed catch test checks actual delivery.

slides.title: Worked example: thirty seconds
body: 4 L/h × 2 emitters × 30 seconds / 3600
0.0667 L ≈ 66.7 mL per plant.
slides.narration: Our completed watering event lasts thirty seconds. Two emitters at four litres per hour give eight litres per hour per plant. There are three thousand six hundred seconds in an hour. Multiply eight by thirty, then divide by three thousand six hundred. That is about zero point zero six six seven litres, or sixty-six point seven millilitres per plant.

visual.caption: Teaching example. Numbers are not recommended crop settings.

workedExample.prompt: Estimate one 30-second event with two 4 L/h emitters for each of 12 plants.
steps: Per-plant flow: 4 × 2 = 8 L/h.
Per-plant delivery: 8 × 30 / 3600 = 1/15 L ≈ 66.7 mL.
Zone delivery: (1/15) × 12 = 0.8 L.
workedExample.answer: Approximately 66.7 mL per plant and exactly 0.8 L per zone at the stated constant flow and runtime.

slides.title: Scale from one plant to twelve
body: Use the unrounded per-plant result.
At 45 seconds: 0.1 L/plant × 20 plants = 2 L/zone; ten identical events = 20 L.
slides.narration: The zone has twelve plants. Multiply the unrounded per-plant amount by twelve. The result is zero point eight litres for the whole zone. Per plant and per zone describe different scopes. For a longer shot at the same flow, the estimated volume rises in proportion to runtime. For a daily total, use completed events rather than every projected event on a plan.

slides.narration: Compare a separate forty-five-second shot using those same two emitters. It delivers zero point one litres, or one hundred millilitres per plant. In five litres of substrate, that volume is two percent of substrate volume. It does not promise a two-point VWC rise. Water can spread unevenly or drain, and the probe samples only part of the container.

slides.title: Five functions, not a shopping spree
body: Host · measure · deliver · control · prove
Start with one zone.
slides.narration:
Start with one zone: plants whose water delivery is controlled together. Prove that small system works before expanding.

Think of watering by hand: you need somewhere to make the plan, a way to check wetness, a water supply, a way to start and stop it, and checks against mistakes. An automated system needs those same five functions.

visual.title: Five functions, not a shopping spree
visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Host and measurement paths
body: Choose one host; verify the probe
The host is the computer that runs the software.
slides.narration:
Every app needs a computer to run on. Here that computer is called the host. Choose one supported route: a Raspberry Pi, or a dedicated Intel NUC or other x86-64 computer. You only need one.

Like any computer, the host needs the correct power supply, suitable storage for its software and data, and a reliable network connection.

The two host lessons are alternative routes to the same starting point. Follow the one for your chosen computer.

Think of labels on a switchboard: one label identifies a reading or a control. Home Assistant calls these named items entities. Crop Steering uses those entities. You need both the Crop Steering integration and the separate Controller app; a dashboard display alone cannot run irrigation. The integration holds room settings and the workspace. The Controller reads those settings and decides when to water.

The moisture probe is the system's local wetness check. Choose a model suitable for the substrate and a position that represents the zone. Verify its exact model, connection interface and units, rather than buying on appearance.

Some probes need a bridge: equipment that translates their connection into one the system can use. Matching wire colours do not prove compatibility. One working probe cannot prove equal delivery to every pot.

EC needs a location label too. Bulk substrate EC describes a measurement through the substrate region; pore-water EC describes the water between solids. Feed EC describes the solution supplied to the crop. Check what the sensor actually measures.

A tank reading stays a tank reading when you rename its label. Calling feed EC root-zone EC cannot move the measurement into the pot.

Air temperature and humidity help explain changing water demand, just as laundry dries differently on a hot, dry day than a cool, damp one.

slides.title: Draw the actual water path
body: A pump is conditional
The next function is water delivery.
slides.narration:
Trace water from its source, as you would trace a garden hose. A suitable pressurised supply may feed a zone valve directly. A reservoir needs a pump if it cannot provide the required pressure.

Do not add a pump just because a diagram has one. If your water path requires a pump, include that pump and the protection suited to it.

Follow the whole path: filtration, pressure regulation, drainage, and protection against reverse flow or unwanted siphoning. These must suit the actual equipment and meet applicable local requirements.

visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

slides.title: Safe control and proof
body: Measure delivery. Prove stopping.
The next function is safe control.
slides.narration:
Starting a pump can demand more power than keeping it running, like the extra push needed to get a loaded trolley moving. Control hardware needs suitable starting and operating ratings and correct installation. A household smart plug's large printed rating alone does not prove suitability.

Use an appropriately qualified installer for electrical work. Do not do mains electrical work as part of this course.

Two people turning the same tap can defeat each other's instructions. Give each physical pump or valve one controller. An old irrigation system must not also operate that output.

Find and resolve competing control before enabling the new Controller.

The final function is protection and proof. Provide an accessible physical shutdown, suitable independent protection and somewhere safe to collect test water. Software OFF is like a stop request on a screen; it is not an emergency isolator.

Use collection cups and a stopwatch to measure what actually arrives. Then observe the outlet after the stop command: the water must physically stop.

A changed dashboard icon is a report from software. Look at the water outlet to prove stopping.

visual.caption: Concept illustration. Any numerical settings are teaching examples.

body: Build one proven zone first
Tank level, feed EC, pH, and tank temperature give useful operating information.
slides.narration: Build the basic working zone before adding instruments. Tank level, feed EC, pH, which describes acidity, and tank temperature add operating information. More probes and a verified flow meter can follow. Automated dosing, thermal cameras and artificial intelligence are not needed for the first working zone.

slides.narration:
Sketch your water route like a simple road map. Label the supply, pump if installed, zone valve, drippers and drainage path.

Beside that map, draw the probe and the Controller. Mark the physical shutdown and identify the one controller responsible for each output.

Circle each item that you cannot identify.

Check exact models using the equipment sheet before buying. Choose the host lesson for your Raspberry Pi or x86-64 computer.

Both host routes then join the same setup procedure: install one zone, assign its sensor readings and water controls, and verify physical operation before adding more zones.

slides.narration: First test the tap and hose, then test the automatic instructions. These are separate commissioning stages. In stage one, Crop Steering Watering stays OFF while the installer uses an approved equipment-level procedure. OFF blocks Controller test shots too; do not try to bypass it. Then check units and measurement types, including which EC is displayed. Inspect the recorded dates and coverage. A full week and one day offer different opportunities for water use. Missing periods stay missing, rather than becoming zeros.

body: Same zone definition; complete matched day-ten records.
A: 12 L estimated; B: 15 L estimated.
B reports 3 L more estimated delivery.
slides.narration: Two fictional runs have complete day-ten records for the same zone definition. Run A reports twelve litres estimated delivery. Run B reports fifteen. Subtract twelve from fifteen: B reports three litres more estimated delivery for that matched day. Preserve the word estimated. These totals cannot tell us that plants absorbed three litres more or that a changed target caused the difference.

Check complete coverage and estimate sources.
Subtract 15 − 12 = 3 L.
Preserve the estimate label and avoid attributing cause.
workedExample.answer: Run B has 3 L more reported estimated delivery for that interval; uptake and cause are not established.

body: A reference is a comparison value or configuration.
A saved snapshot has a capture time.
Creating an old run today cannot reconstruct past targets.
slides.narration: A reference is a comparison value or configuration, like the budget beside the statement. A saved run can preserve a timestamped snapshot of its reference. Creating last month’s run record today captures today’s available reference, unless an existing saved reference is available. It cannot reconstruct last month’s targets or deleted readings. Read the reference source and capture date beside the actual trace.

body: Runtime × configured flow estimates delivery.
Per-plant figures are averages based on plant count.
slides.narration: Complete the sentence: runtime multiplied by configured flow estimates delivery, rather than plant what? Pause. The answer is uptake: water entering the plant. A per-plant figure also averages the zone total over its plant count. It does not prove every emitter supplied equally. Keep estimated, measured or unknown beside the source when you copy values into a report.

slides.narration: Now one record covers day six only; another covers days one through six. An EC series is missing. Decide whether their totals are directly comparable before calculating. They are not. Choose a matched interval with adequate coverage. Write one supported observation and one unanswered question. A longer chart axis cannot recover data the recorder no longer retains.

Then name other possible influences: climate, plant count, flow assumptions and other changes. Finish your practice with scope, interval, units, source and coverage limits. Those details let the next person assess the comparison and choose the next useful check.

options.text: Every target used last month.
options.feedback: A current snapshot cannot reconstruct earlier targets.

options.text: Run metadata and an available timestamped reference.
options.feedback: Correct. Historical readings and targets require their own retained evidence.

options.text: A backdated irrigation start.
options.feedback: Run records start no shots and cannot alter past operations.

options.text: Measured plant uptake.
options.feedback: Runtime and flow estimate delivery, not uptake.

options.text: Proof of equal emitter delivery.
options.feedback: The per-plant result is an average; uniformity needs physical evidence.

options.text: Estimated average delivery per plant.
options.feedback: Correct. Keep both estimate and average labels when using the number.

options.text: First choose a matched interval with adequate coverage.
options.feedback: Correct. Different windows cannot directly support the same total comparison.

options.text: Divide both by plant count and compare immediately.
options.feedback: Per-plant conversion does not repair unequal time coverage.

options.text: Treat the missing days as zero.
options.feedback: A missing record is not evidence of zero delivery.

options.text: The change definitely caused higher uptake.
options.feedback: Neither causal attribution nor uptake is established.

options.text: State the delivery difference and inspect other variables.
options.feedback: Correct. Examine climate, age, flow assumptions and other changes before attributing cause.

options.text: The current reference proves the previous target.
options.feedback: A present reference does not document which target was used historically.

lessons.title: Troubleshoot before you change a recipe
lessons.summary: Separate uncontrolled physical flow from bad information, restore trustworthy evidence and verify the actual repair.
outcomes: Choose physical shutdown first for uncontrolled water.
Investigate four-hour-old moisture and conflicting tank indications without bypassing protections.
Define controller acknowledgement and separate it from saved setup and physical commissioning.
Write a fault report and verify recovery.

slides.title: Repair the evidence before turning the dial
body: Uncontrolled water: use the physical shutdown procedure first.
A target edit cannot repair a sensor or pipe.
slides.narration: Imagine a fridge thermometer with a dead battery. Turning the thermostat does not repair the missing measurement. Apply that idea to irrigation faults. First check for uncontrolled water or unsafe equipment. If water continues unexpectedly, use the installation’s physical shutdown procedure immediately. Once safe, preserve what happened. For a faulty reading without uncontrolled flow, investigate the source through the local fallback procedure.

slides.title: Worked example: a four-hour-old reading
body: Moisture observation is four hours old; zone is holding.
Check identity, source, communications and independent evidence.
slides.narration: A fictional zone is holding and its moisture observation is four hours old. Lowering a threshold would leave the old information unresolved. Record the room, zone, timestamp and hold reason. Check the mapped source, communication path and probe condition under the local procedure. Use appropriate independent evidence with competent help. Verify fresh observations and recovered status before reconsidering targets.

steps: Confirm scope and preserve the timestamp and reason.
Inspect the mapped source and communications.
Use installed safe fallback and independent checks with competent help.
Verify fresh readings and recovered status.
workedExample.answer: Investigate sensing and mapping; do not lower the floor, bypass the hold or force an output.

slides.title: Conflicting tank evidence needs a real check
body: Tank display: 80%; installed low-level indication: low.
Supply readiness remains unresolved.
slides.narration: The tank display says eighty percent, but the installed low-level indication says low. These conflict. Averaging them invents a level; choosing eighty because it is reassuring leaves the fault unresolved. Keep protections in use. Check physical level safely, then source identity, calibration and timestamps. Starting the pump is not a test for an empty tank. Record which evidence resolves the disagreement.

body: Saved: configuration stored.
Acknowledgement: controller confirms the setup revision it accepted.
Commissioning: prove the correct outlets operate and stop.
slides.narration: Saving setup confirms that configuration was stored. Acknowledgement means the controller reports which setup revision it accepted. Check that acceptance, its current heartbeat and setup problems; a heartbeat is a recent communication report. Keep affected watering disabled until acceptance is resolved under the local procedure. Competent commissioning must still prove device identity, the intended outlet’s operation and actual stopping.

slides.narration: The screen says OFF but water is visibly flowing. Finish the first response: physical shutdown. After the installation is safe, competent help can investigate a sticking valve, siphon, incorrect mapping or competing control owners. Header Stop all is a selected-room software action. A returned OFF state cannot prove stopped flow. Disarm and plan hold also cannot replace the physical procedure.

slides.narration: A selected zone shows no water-content rise after an event, while its neighbour rises. Write the observation before naming a cause. Check zone identities, timestamps and commissioning records; consider placement and delivery. Arrange supported equipment checks with competent help rather than forcing valves in turn. Report room, zone, event time, expected result and actual result. Exclude credentials from the report.

body: Make safe → preserve evidence → investigate → verify.
Check recovered readings and the agreed physical final state.
slides.narration: Teach the sequence without looking: make safe, preserve evidence, investigate, verify. Explain how a sensor repair differs from a target adjustment. Verification includes recovered readings and the agreed physical final state, with supervised recommissioning where needed. State any local shutdown knowledge you still need from the responsible operator. Finish with the fault record, the repair evidence and the person responsible for the next check.

quiz.prompt: The app says OFF but water still flows. What comes first?

options.text: Disarm and wait for lights-on.
options.feedback: Disarm is a scheduled handover, not a response to uncontrolled flow.

options.text: Use the installation’s physical shutdown procedure.
options.feedback: Correct. Make the installation safe, then investigate physical and software causes.

options.text: Lower the emergency floor.
options.feedback: A threshold edit cannot safely stop uncontrolled physical flow.

quiz.prompt: Old moisture causes a hold. What is appropriate?

options.text: Restore trustworthy sensing through the safe procedure.
options.feedback: Correct. Verify source, communications and recovery before target changes.

options.text: Bypass the hold and force a shot.
options.feedback: That removes protection while evidence remains unreliable.

options.text: Lower the floor until it clears.
options.feedback: A safety-reference edit cannot make an old reading trustworthy.

quiz.prompt: A tank percentage conflicts with low-level indication. What should you do?

options.text: Trust the higher value and start the pump.
options.feedback: The reassuring value does not resolve the contradiction or prove safe supply.

options.text: Average the two readings.
options.feedback: Averaging conflicting sources invents a level rather than verifying it.

options.text: Verify level and sources safely, keeping protections.
options.feedback: Correct. Treat readiness as unresolved until physical and source checks resolve it.

options.text: Correct outlets have been commissioned.
options.feedback: Saving, and even acknowledgement alone, cannot prove physical operation.

options.text: Storage succeeded; controller acceptance is unresolved.
options.feedback: Correct. Check revision acceptance and keep affected watering disabled until resolved.

options.text: The mappings are safe to test by forced output.
options.feedback: Use supervised commissioning instead of bypassing controls.

lessons.title: A five-minute daily check and a useful handover
lessons.summary: Use a short preflight and a clear diary to make one defensible decision, then leave a handover another operator can use.
outcomes: Complete the five-part daily record with source labels and unknowns.
Record a justified no-change decision or a reviewed change and follow-up.
Use Crop AI as assistance while checking evidence and protecting credentials.
Explain local handover, recoverable backups and later recall.

slides.title: A short preflight, then a brief diary
body: Five parts: identity/freshness; state; water; feed/context; decision.
The record helps the next operator understand your decision.
slides.narration: A pilot checks the aircraft before departure, then records the flight. Use the same rhythm for the daily check: inspect first, leave a brief diary afterwards. The record has five parts: identity and freshness; state; water; feed and context; decision. Five minutes is a useful routine, not a deadline for an unresolved fault. Record unavailable sources explicitly.

slides.title: Fill the first four parts with evidence
body: Identity: room, zone, time and source ages.
State: phase, reason and last event.
Water: source-labelled delivery. Feed/context: tank, EC type and relevant conditions.
slides.narration: Start with room, zone, time and ages of the controller and relevant probes. State means the phase, Why / next action, last irrigation and confirmed output reports. Water means the delivery total and any per-plant average, labelled measured, estimated or unknown. Feed and context means tank indications, the EC measurement type and relevant crop or climate notes. These give the final decision a basis.

body: Training North / Zone 3; recent reports and expected maintenance.
Delivery labelled estimated; tank indications agree.
No change; record the reason and next check time.
slides.narration: In a fictional paper example, training North, Zone three, has recent reports, the expected maintenance phase and a clear waiting reason. Estimated delivery is within its recent observed range. Tank indications agree. The decision can be no change. Write that reason and when you will check again. The value of the check is a defensible decision. Moving a slider is not a required outcome.

steps: Confirm identity and freshness.
Read phase and decision reason.
Label delivery and inspect tank/context evidence.
Record a justified no-change decision and next check.
workedExample.answer: No. Keeping targets can be a reasoned decision; record its evidence and follow-up.

slides.title: Your turn: finish the change record
body: Scope, before/after, reason and expected observation.
Draft → Review → Apply → Readback → Follow-up.
slides.narration: For a justified change, record scope, before and after, reason and the observation you expect next. A draft is the proposed edit. Review checks it, apply sends it, and readback checks the returned accepted value. Complete the sequence with a follow-up time. If several things change, record them all. One better day cannot isolate which change caused the difference.
